Preprint · bioRxiv 2026

Text2WetLab: Benchmarking Large Language Model Agents on Opentrons OT-2 Protocol Generation

Niall O'Leary1, Mohammed Alshehri2  ·  1PhysicalAI Benchmarks  ·  2Independent (Devin AI)
Correspondence: niall@physicalai.io  ·  github.com/PhysicalAIBenchmarks/Text2WetLab

Abstract

We introduce Text2WetLab, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agent performance on automated wet-lab protocol generation. Seven Opentrons OT-2 tasks—spanning single-step liquid transfers to 33-step multi-reagent assemblies—are graded by a dual-layer evaluator: a deterministic simulator gate (opentrons_simulate + end-state checks) and a task-specific LLM rubric judge (claude-sonnet-5-5). We evaluate Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Fable 5.1 as Claude Code agents in isolated Modal sandboxes (pass@1). All 21 trials produced syntactically valid, simulator-passing protocols; all deterministic checks passed. Score differentiation came entirely from the LLM judge. Mean rewards: Opus 5.5 = 0.935, Sonnet 5.5 = 0.910, Fable 5.1 = 0.882. E. coli heat-shock transformation was the hardest task for all models (mean 0.762), driven by a universal tendency to add unrequested post-DNA-addition mixing steps. Golden Gate assembly was solved perfectly by all three. We release tasks, graders, protocols, and per-item judge evidence.

1   Introduction

Liquid-handling robots have become essential infrastructure in modern biology. The Opentrons OT-2 executes Python protocols that fully specify reagent transfers, volumes, tip changes, and labware layout. Writing these protocols is a manual, error-prone task requiring both domain biology knowledge and Opentrons API fluency. Large language models have demonstrated impressive code generation and scientific reasoning capabilities—but can an LLM agent, given natural-language procedure description, produce a runnable, correct, and safe OT-2 protocol?

Existing benchmarks for biological AI focus on sequence understanding, structure prediction, or literature retrieval. No public benchmark evaluates end-to-end wet-lab protocol generation at the robotic execution level. Text2WetLab fills this gap with a two-stage evaluation: (1) a deterministic gate using the Opentrons simulator and a deck-state checker verifying exact liquid volumes; (2) a task-specific rubric judge evaluating protocol quality along biologically meaningful dimensions—pipette strategy, contamination avoidance, robot practice, and procedural fidelity to the source paper.

2.2   Dual-Layer Grader (Mo Alshehri's Contribution)

Each task is graded by a two-stage pipeline. Stage 1 (deterministic): protocol_lint.py blocks forbidden operations (answer-key reads, result forgery), opentrons_simulate validates runtime correctness, and spec_check.py verifies exact labware end-states. Stage 2 (LLM judge): claude-sonnet-5-5 scores 5–9 task-specific rubric items (0 / 0.5 / 1). The judge receives simulator verdicts as ground truth facts; it cannot override them. Final reward = (deterministic_reward + judge_mean) / 2.

Mo Alshehri authored the per-task rubrics (rubric.json) and judge harness (judge_layer.py) for all six deterministic tasks, extending the judge-only design of the RNA extraction task to the full suite. He also updated the task.toml schema to Harbor 1.4 with [verifier] env = {ANTHROPIC_API_KEY} and [environment] network_mode = "allowlist", enabling the judge to call the Anthropic API from inside the sandbox.

2.3   Agent Setup and Security

Agents ran as claude-code in Harbor sandboxes on Modal (pass@1). The sandbox: Python 3.10, opentrons 7.5.0, Claude Code CLI, network limited to api.anthropic.com. Grader scripts mount only after agent exit. protocol_lint.py blocks seven jailbreak categories: answer-key reads, result forgery, log-parser patching, dunder escapes, import-os-and-exit, comment-spoof, and system-exit-after-forge.

5   Per-Task Discussion

a1-a12-100ul
1 pipetting step · handwritten · p300 · tip economy test
Opus 1.000 ✓ Sonnet 0.917 Fable 0.833

Transfer 100 µL from a 195 mL reservoir to each of wells A1–A12 of a 96-well plate. Despite apparent simplicity, this task probes two discriminating agent behaviours: correct pipette selection (p300 for 100 µL, not the p20) and tip economy (one tip reused across a single-reagent transfer into empty wells is best practice).

Opus 5.5 was perfect: one tip, correct pipette, clean loop. Sonnet 5.5 (−0.083) changed tips after each well—safe but wasteful; the judge scored tip_usage = 0.5. Fable 5.1 (−0.167) additionally left flow rates at defaults and omitted a metadata block, drawing a robot_practice = 0.5 deduction. All three protocols were biologically correct; the spread is entirely OT-2 engineering discipline.

All models solved the biology. The 0.167-point spread reflects tip economy and metadata hygiene, not correctness.
split-200ul-two-wells
1 step · handwritten · 2 destinations
Opus 1.000 ✓ Sonnet 1.000 ✓ Fable 0.917

Split 200 µL from a reservoir into two wells (A1 and B1). The p300 holds 300 µL; the task can be solved with either two transfers or a single distribute call. Opus and Sonnet both achieved perfect scores. Fable's sole deduction was robot_practice = 0.5 for absence of a protocol comment block.

Two of three models achieved perfection. Confirms the benchmark lower bound is well-calibrated.
ampure-bead-cleanup
13 steps · pioneer-ngs · 96 wells · magnetic module · 0.8× bead ratio
Opus 0.944 Sonnet 0.889 Fable 1.000 ✓

AMPure XP bead cleanup: add 40 µL beads per well (96 wells), incubate, engage magnet, remove supernatant, two 200 µL ethanol washes, air-dry, disengage, add 50 µL water, re-elute, transfer 45 µL eluate. The magnetic module engagement steps cannot be simulated and are recorded as protocol.comment() placeholders. This tests ordered multi-step execution with implicit biological context about aspiration heights near pellets.

Fable 5.1 was the only model to achieve a perfect score—a notable inversion from simpler tasks where Opus led. Fable used fresh tips wherever different samples were touched and selected appropriate 1–2 mm bottom aspiration heights to avoid disturbing magnetic pellets. Opus 5.5 (−0.056) was penalised solely for default near-bottom aspirations over the pellet. Sonnet 5.5 (−0.111) additionally used 30 µL × 10 as the elution mix rather than the specified 50 µL—an arithmetic failure leaving beads partially unresuspended.

Fable's perfect score on the most complex procedural task challenges the assumption that larger models always win. The shared robot_practice deduction across Opus and Sonnet reflects a gap in tacit knowledge about magnetic-module aspiration heights—knowledge not given in the task spec.
colony-pcr-screening
4 steps · slowpoke + apex · master-mix distribution · cross-contamination critical
Opus 1.000 ✓ Sonnet 0.875 Fable 0.875

Distribute PCR master mix, add colony template DNA from individual tubes, add forward and reverse primers, record thermocycling comment. The critical concern: cross-contamination. Each colony DNA source must receive a fresh tip; reusing tips transfers DNA between colony samples, producing false positives.

Opus 5.5 handled this perfectly. Both Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5.1 scored 0.875, both losing tips_and_contamination = 0.5 and robot_practice = 0.5. The judge noted "a tip is reused across template additions without justification; in colony PCR, cross-contamination between colony DNA sources is the primary failure mode." Crucially, the deterministic grader did not catch this—volumes were correct. Only the judge layer identified the safety issue.

Both Sonnet and Fable made the same cross-contamination error. In a real deployment, incorrect tip reuse in colony PCR wastes an entire plate run. This demonstrates the necessity of the LLM judge layer.
ecoli-heat-shock-transformation
4 pipetting steps · apex · hardest task · mean 0.762 · universal phantom-mix failure
Opus 0.714 Sonnet 0.857 Fable 0.714

Add 2 µL plasmid DNA to competent cells, heat-shock at 42°C for 45 seconds (recorded as protocol.comment()), place on ice 2 minutes, add 250 µL SOC recovery medium. The key constraint is what the robot should not do: mixing competent cells after DNA addition disrupts the cell membrane and drastically reduces transformation efficiency.

Universal failure — phantom mix step: Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 both added an unrequested mix_after=(3,10) parameter to the DNA addition transfer. Judge evidence: "mix_after=(3,10) mixes competent cells with 3 aspirate-dispense cycles at 10 µL, which mechanically disrupts the cells and is not in the task." This is a hallucinated step—models' training data for transformation protocols overwhelmingly contains mixing steps that are appropriate for other contexts but contraindicated here. Both scored dna_addition = 0.5 and fidelity_to_task = 0.5.

Universal failure — heat shock comment: All three models collapsed heat-shock and ice steps into a single protocol.comment() rather than two separate comments with operator pauses. All scored heat_shock = 0.5. Sonnet 5.5 (0.857) avoided the phantom mix, correctly transferring DNA without mechanical mixing, yielding the highest score on this task.

The phantom mix is a critical biological error. Adding mix_after to competent cells would waste expensive cells in a real experiment and could fail a cloning workflow entirely. The 0.143-point gap between Sonnet and Opus/Fable on this task is the largest model-to-model difference in the benchmark.
golden-gate-assembly
33 steps · assemblytron · all models perfect · most specified task
Opus 1.000 ✓ Sonnet 1.000 ✓ Fable 1.000 ✓

PCR setup, DpnI digest and cleanup, Golden Gate ligation mix, thermocycler programming, and bacterial transformation across 33 ordered pipetting actions. All three models achieved perfect scores. This apparent paradox—the most step-rich task is the easiest—has a clear explanation: the task brief provides exact quantities, ordered steps, and named destinations for every action with no biological ambiguity. The judge rubric rewards literal specification fidelity, which all models delivered. Code generation capability handles 33-step complexity without difficulty; tacit biological knowledge is what discriminates.

Task difficulty is not determined by step count. Highly specified tasks are solved perfectly regardless of length. Ambiguity about biological best practices—not code complexity—is the primary failure mode.
opentrons-rna-extraction
48 samples · hulp-rna-extraction · 16 deterministic checks + LLM judge · SARS-CoV-2
Opus 0.889 Sonnet 0.833 Fable 0.833

Automated SARS-CoV-2 RNA extraction for 48 samples using magnetic beads (hulp-rna-extraction, used clinically at Leiden UMC during COVID-19). Graded by 16 explicitly enumerated run-log checks rather than declarative end-state spec. All models passed all 16 checks—a strong result for a clinically validated protocol.

Universal failure — elution recovery volume: The source protocol specifies aspirating ~80 µL from a 100 µL elution (leaving ~20 µL behind to avoid disturbing the bead pellet). All three models aspirated 100 µL. Judge evidence: "recovering 100 µL instead of ~80 µL risks transferring bead pellet material into the eluate, which would inhibit downstream RT-qPCR." In a COVID-19 diagnostic context, this could produce false-negative results. Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5.1 additionally lost fidelity_to_paper = 0.5 for omitting the elution mixing step and minor step-order deviations.

The 100 µL vs 80 µL recovery error is consistent and consequential. It represents a systematic gap between generic protocol training data (aspirate all the eluate) and clinical practitioner knowledge (leave a safety margin). This is a real failure mode for diagnostic deployment.

6   Cross-Cutting Findings

6.1   Sim Pass = 100%; All Failures Are Semantic

All 21 agent trials passed opentrons_simulate without error, and all deterministic end-state checks passed. Syntactic and structural correctness of OT-2 protocols is a solved problem for frontier models. The challenge is semantic quality: biological best practices, contamination awareness, and clinical-protocol fidelity.

6.2   robot_practice Is the Universal Weak Point

robot_practice was penalised in 11 of 21 trials (52%). It encodes wet-lab tacit knowledge: aspiration heights near pellets, flow rates for sensitive materials, protocol pauses for operator steps, metadata quality. This dimension is almost never explicit in specifications—it exists only in practitioner experience and published best-practices documentation. The LLM judge is the only evaluator that captures it.

6.3   Model Ranking Is Task-Dependent

Opus 5.5 leads overall (0.935) but Fable 5.1 outperforms it on AMPure cleanup (1.0 vs 0.944). Sonnet 5.5 leads on E. coli heat-shock (0.857 vs 0.714). No model dominates all biological niches—a routing layer selecting model by task type could outperform any single model.

6.4   Cost-Efficiency

Sonnet 5.5 achieves 97.3% of Opus 5.5's mean score at 33% of the cost ($0.41 vs $1.25 for the full 7-task eval). Fable 5.1 was most expensive ($3.69) while scoring lowest. For high-throughput protocol generation, Sonnet 5.5 is the clear cost-performance winner.

6.5   The Necessity of the LLM Judge Layer

The most safety-relevant failures—competent cell mixing in heat-shock, cross-contamination in colony PCR, eluate volume in RNA extraction—were invisible to the deterministic grader. All protocols passed all binary checks. Without the rubric judge, Text2WetLab would report all models as near-perfect, masking clinically and experimentally significant errors. Mo Alshehri's judge layer is the methodologically critical contribution that makes the benchmark meaningful.

7   Conclusion

Text2WetLab shows that frontier LLM agents reliably generate syntactically and structurally correct OT-2 protocols across biological complexity levels. The meaningful evaluation frontier has shifted to semantic quality: biological best practices, contamination avoidance, and procedural fidelity to source literature.

Our key contributions: (1) a dual-layer benchmark grader capturing safety-relevant failures invisible to deterministic evaluation; (2) per-item judge evidence making failure modes interpretable and actionable; (3) three-model evaluation establishing performance baselines with cost analysis; (4) MuJoCo 3D renders enabling visual comparison of oracle and agent trajectories; (5) an open-source framework for extension to new tasks and instruments.

Future work: expansion to non-Opentrons instruments (Hamilton, Tecan Fluent, BMG CLARIOstar), multi-agent workflows for complex multi-day experiments, and pass@k evaluation quantifying reliability for production deployment.
